source_text:
AI isn't (for the foreseeable future) a superintelligence, certainly not one with its own motives. Right now AI exists to do two things: - sidesteppin
AI isn't (for the foreseeable future) a superintelligence, certainly not one with its own motives. Right now AI exists to do two things: - sidestepping legal and regulatory inconveniences like copyright (which drives a massive chunk of investment the same way crypto did by sidestepping financial regulations, AirBnB did by sidestepping housing regulations, Uber did by sidestepping passenger transport regulations and it and the various delivery and other "gig work" apps did by sidestepping labor laws) - drastically reducing the cost of (and drastically lowering the bar in terms of skillset and effort for) churning out large amounts of low to medium quality assets/code, saturating various systems designed to pay for intellectual property (e.g. ad or subscription based music/video streaming apps with revenue sharing programs, but also literally any form of digital contract work at almost any scale of business) Neither of these are helping people (in general) and in fact they're extremely destructive (or "disruptive" if you want to make it sound positive) to the existing systems society relies on because they became feasible and (thanks to massive private subsidies, aka "investments", by VC firms and extremely creative accounting) very affordable  extremely  quickly. What's worse - while it seems extremely likely that most of the AI generated "works" aren't actually considered copyrightable works by law and it's entirely possible that the use of copyright-protected works in training data does in fact not violate copyright, this does not in fact create a "world without copyright" because IP laws continue to exist and continue to apply, they just no longer meaningfully protect creative labor (i.e. anyone whose profession relies on producing works, whether that's an artist or a programmer) because anything they produce can be cheaply mass reproduced while they still have to stay clear of claims of anyone with enough funds to enforce rights against them. Under the current economic system there are exactly four ways to earn money to buy back a share of society's resources to sustain your own life (let alone that of your dependents, e.g. kids or aging/impaired parents/spouses/family members): 1. Simple labor: you generally get paid based on your output or a very low flat day rate conditional to maintaining a measurable level of performance. This is typically "low-skilled" menial production labor. Much of this has been replaced by automation in factories and offices alike and most of what couldn't be automated has been moved into countries with fewer labor protections and a higher supply of desperate people willing to accept what are often bad working conditions because cost of labor is usually one of the biggest contributor to overall production cost. In "the West", this kind of work is now scarce and even when it's relatively safe it's often exhausting and unrewarding. A traditional example would be a seamstress or factory line worker, a more modern example would be someone working in visual effects overseas or content moderation / AI training. How much money you can make is ultimately limited by the physical limitations of how much output you can produce per waking/working hour. For the entrepreneurial-minded this would also include people selling their home-made goods on sites like etsy. 2. Time-based: this can be anything from a masseuse to a lawyer or technician. Unlike simple labor the only relevant metric here is time spent. Although employment contracts may specify a fixed wage or at least a fixed component, the understanding is still that this fixed amount is conditional to a minimum average amount of billable time provided. Most employment contracts specify an expected number of working hours for various reasons but we're specifically talking about jobs where the output from the worker to the customer is "billable time". Arguably most service work (e.g. barristas, store clerks, waitresses, performers/mascots in amusement parks) also falls into this category because while customers often don't directly pay for access time the understanding is that you are paid to perform a certain role for the duration of the opening hours (i.e. act like a friendly, welcoming host or assistant). How much money you can make is directly tied to how much time you can spend working or justify billing. 3. Assets: you produce or buy works/products and lend/license them for use. This is in part where a lot of the original "gig work" lived (e.g. facilitating "couch surfing" or renting out your spare lawnmower) but also includes many simple rental businesses and arguably also landlords. The limiting factor here is the starting capital required to produce or buy things in the first place. Physical assets often also come with storage and maintenance overhead whereas software licensing often comes with expectations of continuing maintenance updates or improvements. Note that software inherently lives in this category rather than the first because unless you're selling away exclusive rights (such as usually required by the terms of employment contracts for wage labor) you only ever sell  licenses , not the software itself. 4. Capital: although I said landlords arguably belong in the previous category, real estate traders/investors definitely belong in this one. The idea here is that you don't need to produce anything, you don't need to spend certain amounts of time, you don't need to produce or buy anything substantial and facilitate its use, you make your money entirely in the abstract. Whether it's margin trading, investing in derivatives or holding company stock until you sell it when the line has gone up far enough. The easiest way to make signficant amounts of money reliably is to start with many orders of magnitude more than what you want to make so that percentile gains are still significant - or that you can make enough risky high-risk high-reward bets for the occasional successful moonshot to offset the losses. Nowadays in many countries retirement funds are tied to the stock market, so in a way most people participate in this in some way but actually earning an "income" this way requires access to significant amounts of capital. Advances in technology and especially low cost of transport and thus access to cheap labor overseas have significantly drained the ability for most people to earn their living via category 1. While there was a short-lived boom in "DIY retail" that one (alongside much of traditional retail) has largely been drowned out by white label dropshipping thanks to the disinterest from platforms like Amazon which are now flooded by nearly identical copies of the same knock-off doodads you can also find on Temu and Alibaba (respectively at decreasing fractions of the price). Despite some astroturf campaigns trying to sell you on believing otherwise so they can run away with your money after the next cryptocurrency rugpull, category 4 isn't really a meaningful option for the vast majority of people although it can sometimes be a good way to slowly grow excess wealth (i.e. money you don't currently need and ideally can afford to lose) - but that still narrows it down to a small segment of the overall population. Category 2 used to be a jumping off point to category 3: you work overtime, save up the extra income to buy or rent a studio or office or equipment or factory, or to be able to afford to take some time off to develop and launch your own asset (or SaaS) - it's how many startups with technical founders started out and it's literally the "American Dream". But hourly wages have mostly stagnated (or even decreased) relative to the rising cost of living (even more so if you include expenses expected to "participate in society", which naturally also often increase with the income bracket of your peer group - or the parents of your kid's peer group if you have kids). And now AI is coming along and just like cheap white label dropshipping of knock-off goods turned out to be the more successful strategy for taking advantage of the technological innovations believed to make it easier to launch your own physical products (via 3D printing, cheap overseas sourcing of parts, online advertising, etc), AI has turned out to be the more successful strategy for taking advantage of platforms and schemes marketed as making it easier to launch your own digital services - in addition to completely eliminating the market for paid "just good enough" quality digital assets, such as the kind of work found on sites like Fiverr or Upwork, i.e. the kind of work that often provided early experience to professionals not yet qualified or confident enough to take on higher paid work.

source_text:
Bug: Wait node with "Respond When: Form Is Submitted" delays the response until downstream nodes finish
### Bug Description

The Wait node does not seem to respond to a form submission immediately when the Respond When option is set to Form Is Submitted.

The behavior appears to depend on whether the Wait node has downstream nodes connected to it. If there are no downstream nodes, the form response is sent immediately. However, if the workflow continues through additional nodes, including another Wait node, the form response is delayed until the downstream execution finishes.

This behavior does not seem consistent with the documented purpose of the Form Is Submitted option.

### To Reproduce

1. Create a workflow with a Wait node configured to wait for a form submission.
2. Set Respond When to Form Is Submitted.
3. Submit the form without connecting any downstream nodes to the Wait node.
4. Observe that the form responds immediately.
5. Now connect the first Wait node to several additional nodes, including a second Wait node.
6. Configure the second Wait node to wait for another event or form submission.
7. Submit the form again at the first Wait node.
8. Observe that the response is not sent immediately. Instead, it appears to wait until the downstream nodes finish executing, including the second Wait node.

### Expected behavior

When Respond When is set to Form Is Submitted, the form response should be sent immediately after the form is submitted, regardless of whether downstream nodes continue executing.

Automations: create one, turn it on, and check its first runs
Check setting up a scheduled task on the Automations page.

## Try this

1. Open Automations (app.useagent.org/agent/automations) and choose New automation.
2. What should run: "Daily weather note". Instructions: `Find tomorrow's weather for <your city> and write a three-line note on what to wear.` Cadence: Daily. Set your Timezone.
3. Save it. Note its state, then turn it on.
4. Use Run now once.
5. Wait for its first scheduled run, then open View history.

## What to look for

- It's clear that new automations start paused, and how to turn one on.
- Run now starts a run right away, and you can open it from the history.
- The scheduled run happens at the right local time.
- The card shows when it last ran.
- Leaving a field empty gives a message that makes sense.

## Your report

Post one comment here with:

- Links to your threads (`app.useagent.org/session/...`)
- What worked
- What broke or confused you, and what you expected instead
- Screenshots or a short screen recording

Open a separate bug issue for anything broken, with the steps to reproduce it, and link it in your comment.

No need to claim; post your report as a comment.

---

**General asks**
- Do the steps yourself in the hosted app. Sign up with your email at [app.useagent.org](https://app.useagent.org/login?ref=feedback); you don't need an API key or a card to start. The link in the sign-up email works for 24 hours, so check spam if it's missing.
- Run everything by hand. Reports from runs done or simulated by another AI tool get closed.
- Use made-up details, test accounts and data you own. Don't point the agent at other people's accounts, inboxes or private data, and don't send real forms or messages to strangers.
- More than one person can report on the same issue, and every report helps. If someone already found what you found, add only what's different.
- Stuck? Comment here with a screenshot and we'll help.

**Keep private details out of here**

This page is public. Don't post your real email, phone number, address, API keys, or screenshots that show any of them; blur them first. Send anything private to **hi@useagent.org** with a link to your comment here.

**Using AI tools, and what gets no reply**
- AI help is fine. Blind AI output is not. You must understand every line you submit, run it yourself, and show it working in the app with your own screenshots or recording.
- Pull requests that look generated and untested get closed without a reply and labeled `spam`, which also means they don't count for Hacktoberfest. Signs we look for: no proof from a real run, code that ignores this repo's patterns or reinvents helpers that already exist, unrelated files changed, a description that only restates the issue, and failing checks nobody looked at.
- One pull request per issue, by the person who claimed it. Opening pull requests on issues someone else has taken, or several near-identical pull requests for the same bounty, counts as farming and gets the same treatment.
- Bounties are paid only for the verified outcome the issue describes (for example, a workshop that actually happened, or an app that works on both systems), never for a write-up, a plan, or an unfinished attempt.
- When we ask a question in review, answer it in your own words. If you can't explain your change, we can't merge it.

How does the crowding out work here? I'm not being pedantic, I'm genuinely curious about the dynamics as you see them. My experience in the publishing
How does the crowding out work here? I'm not being pedantic, I'm genuinely curious about the dynamics as you see them. My experience in the publishing world is that there is already an infinite supply of writing. Lots of things serve as filters, some for better and some for worse, but ultimately the quality of the writing (however we define that) vs. the field is part of that filter. There is a competition for our limited little attention spans and finite waking hours, and writing better suited to our tastes tends to win out. I don't see how that dynamic changes with AI. If all writers have more or less equal access to AI, some writers will use it in ways that result in writing I enjoy more than others. Some won't use it at all and still write work I really like. The majority of people writing with or without AI, just as today, won't write stuff I really want to read. I don't know if I've ever read a piece of SEO-driven content marketing and thought it was particularly profound or that it made an impact on me. Or that I really had an inherently meaningful connection to the author. I sort of don't care if people generate 100x more of that sort of thing. It makes Google searches less effective, I guess? Or it may make my For You Page on Instagram less human-rich? I've read some nice poetry though. I usually go looking for it. There are a handful of authors I tend to like consistently. The overall volume of poetry published (it's quite a lot!) doesn't really have an effect on my preference for their work. If there was 1,000,000 times more poetry published because of AI, I don't think it would prevent me from seeking out new poems from writers/publishers/curators I like, nor would I probably really notice.

- Evidence priority: verified internal living archive and standards -> general reasoning -> public web where appropriate; preserve deterministic safety/standards verification, precise citations for verified claims, uncertainty on insufficient evidence.
- **Use -> Extend -> Build**: evaluate native ChatGPT/OpenAI capabilities, GitHub integrations/actions, established libraries and APIs before building bespoke implementations. Avoid duplicating PDF reading/summarization, OCR, Excel execution, document parsing, search, and file management.
- Review newly available tools and connector capabilities at implementation time against cost, security, privacy, vendor lock-in, quality, and maintenance. Do not assume a capability exists or is free until verified.
- Keep elevator.help technical assistance separate from the later commercial **Elevator Agent AI** supplier/parts marketplace. Provide a future handoff interface, not premature marketplace implementation.

## Six starter actions and expected behaviors
1. **Troubleshoot a fault**: ask manufacturer/model/fault code/context; optionally analyze photo/document; provide evidence-based, safety-conscious diagnostics.
2. **Search technical documentation**: retrieve relevant verified internal documentation first; provide grounded answer and citation where permitted; fallback appropriately.
3. **Ask about EN 81-20 / EN 81-50**: retrieve authoritative text, verify clause/numbers deterministically, fail closed on unverified normative claims.
4. **Plan shaft dimensions**: gather capacity, lift type, building constraints; provide clearly labeled preliminary guidance, not certified design.
5. **Send a photo**: inspect image, identify visible objects/labels and uncertainty; ask *what the user wants to do* (identify component, troubleshoot, find manual, find spare part, find supplier). Never infer unseen technical properties.
6. **Upload a document**: securely parse PDF/images/office files as supported, extract text/tables, summarize, answer user questions grounded in the uploaded file; ask intent when ambiguous.

## Proposed phased Gamma work
- **Gamma 1 — Intent and UX:** intelligent starter actions, intent router, follow-up questions, multilingual behavior, mobile scroll/input, clear answer feedback (like/dislike), observability. Reuse existing code.
- **Gamma 2 — Multimodal and documents:** photo analysis, PDF reading/summarization/Q&A, secure temporary uploads, consent for storage, per-user isolation, retention/deletion, size and rate limits, GDPR/privacy and cost budgets. No automatic ingestion of user uploads into shared/public archive.
- **Gamma 3 — Safe calculations:** run approved archived Excel calculation models and user-supplied spreadsheets in sandboxed, isolated execution; validated inputs, formulas, outputs, provenance, resource/time limits; never execute untrusted macros or arbitrary code. Use mature spreadsheet engines/libraries first.
- **Later:** validated Answer Catalog / canonical FAQs with versioned standard revalidation, quotas/metering and optional billing, My Elevator product finder. Supplier/spare-part sourcing remains a future Elevator Agent AI integration via an explicit tool contract.

## Acceptance / design gates
- Real-document end-to-end Living Archive test before Gamma.
- Human Beta test set: technical fault cases, verified standard clauses, ordinary conversational follow-ups, DE/FA/EN, mobile login and Google OAuth, performance/security/cost.
- For each new feature: inventory existing OpenAI/ChatGPT, GitHub, Gemini, Cloudflare and OSS tools; choose use/extend/build with rationale, measured costs and security review; add offline regression tests and production smoke checks.
- No new paid services or production deployment without explicit approval.

## Next action
After Beta is closed, decompose this roadmap into small independent implementation issues, beginning with Gamma 1. Do not start coding from this issue alone.

String .toDate() returns the previous day for a date-only ISO string west of UTC
### Bug Description

`String.toDate()` returns the day **before** the one written when the string is a date-only ISO date (`"2023-06-16"`) and the n8n process runs west of UTC (any `America/*` time zone, for example).

`toDate()` parses with `Date.parse()`, which reads a date-only ISO string as **UTC** midnight, and then forces "00:00h" with `date.setHours(0, 0, 0)`, which works on the **local** fields. In `America/New_York`, `2023-06-16T00:00Z` is `2023-06-15 20:00` local, so `setHours(0, 0, 0)` lands on `2023-06-15 00:00` local. East of UTC (and in UTC) the local day already matches, so the bug only shows up for instances west of UTC.

Other date-only forms such as `"June 16, 2023"` parse as local midnight and are not affected.

The same code is in `packages/workflow/src/extensions/string-extensions.ts` and its mirror in `@n8n/expression-runtime`.

### To Reproduce

1. Run n8n with `TZ=America/New_York` (or `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`/system time zone west of UTC).
2. Evaluate `{{ "2023-06-16".toDate().toDateString() }}` in an expression.
3. You get `Thu Jun 15 2023`.

Minimal Node reproduction of the same steps:

```sh
TZ=America/New_York node -e 'const d = new Date(Date.parse("2023-06-16")); d.setHours(0, 0, 0); console.log(d.toString())'
# Thu Jun 15 2023 00:00:00 GMT-0400 (Eastern Daylight Time)
```

### Expected behavior

`Fri Jun 16 2023`: local midnight of the day that was written, in every time zone.

### Debug Info

Found by reading the code on `master`, and reproduced with a unit test that calls `stringExtensions.functions.toDate` directly with `process.env.TZ = 'America/New_York'`.

### Operating System

Ubuntu Linux

### n8n Version

master (current HEAD)

### Node.js Version

20.19.2

### Database

SQLite (default)

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

self hosted

Junior Python LLM Bot Developer
I need a junior-level Python developer who is excited about building automation bots powered by both offline and online large-language models. The immediate task is to create bots that streamline routine processes for my company and then connect those bots seamlessly to our existing web apps, a couple of legacy desktop tools, and several cloud services we already use.  

You should already be comfortable spinning up SaaS-style back ends (FastAPI, Django, or a similar stack is fine) and have at least tinkered with frameworks such as LangChain, [login to view URL], or the OpenAI API so you can switch between local and hosted LLMs when needed. A solid grasp of common automation libraries—think Selenium, Playwright, PyAutoGUI, or REST hooks—will also make the work smoother.  

Deliverables I expect:  
• A working automation bot (or small fleet of bots) that can log in, collect data, act on it, and hand results back to our web, desktop, and cloud environments without manual intervention.  
• Clear, concise setup instructions and inline code comments so another developer can extend the project later.  
• A brief hand-off call or screen-share so I can see the bot in action and ask final questions.  

If you enjoy experimenting with LLM prompts, integrating APIs, and turning repetitive tasks into one-click workflows, you’ll be a great fit. Let me know what similar projects you’ve already built, especially any that bridged multiple platforms the way this one will.

[software-development-practices:nist-ssdf] github/gh-aw-firewall repository guidance Repository-observable SSDF controls for `github/gh-aw-firewall` are generally strong at commit `360f0f904b1824dbffa1288d8dee58db94e903ab`: pinned GitHub Actions, scheduled CodeQL/dependency/supply-chain scans, SBOM/cosign coverage for container images, and regression-oriented test gates are all present. The main evidence-backed gap is release integrity for non-container CLI assets: I found checksum validation for `awf-*` binaries and `awf.tgz`, but not a repo-observable signature or provenance verification path for those assets themselves. This review is advisory and non-binding; it does not prove security, compliance, certification, endorsement, or SSDF conformance. **Action:** Maintainer should assign this issue to Copilot to add signed or attested verification for CLI release assets and update installer/docs; accept when a release publishes verifiable signatures or provenance for `awf-*` binaries and `awf.tgz`, `install.sh` or setup paths validate them, and release documentation shows the verification flow. - Critical finding: container release integrity is stronger than CLI release integrity today (`.github/workflows/release.yml`, `docs/image-verification.md`, `install.sh`, `docs/releasing.md`). - Critical finding: repository-observable detection and prevention controls are broad and active in source (`.github/workflows/codeql.yml`, `dependency-audit.yml`, `supply-chain-scan.yml`, `test-coverage.yml`, `.github/dependabot.yml`). - Critical metric: 1 promoted backlog item met the threshold for an evidence-backed repository change in this run.
Agent prompt Implement a release-integrity improvement for `github/gh-aw-firewall` focused on SSDF PS.2.1 / PS.3.1 / PS.3.2. Requirements: 1. Extend the release pipeline so `awf-linux-x64`, `awf-linux-arm64`, `awf-darwin-x64`, `awf-darwin-arm64`, `awf-bundle.js`, and `awf.tgz` ship with verifiable signatures or provenance that is generated in CI and published with the release. 2. Update `install.sh` and any setup/install path that currently trusts only `checksums.txt` so it validates the new signature/provenance material before installation, while still failing closed on mismatches. 3. Update release/install docs to show how users verify the CLI assets, parallel to the existing container-image verification guidance. 4. Add or update focused tests that cover failure paths for tampered assets/metadata. 5. Keep existing container signing/SBOM behavior intact. Deliverables: - Workflow changes in `.github/workflows/release.yml` - Installer/setup changes (`install.sh`, `action.yml`, or both as needed) - Documentation updates (`docs/releasing.md`, `README.md`, `docs/image-verification.md` or a better-named CLI verification doc) - Tests proving the verification path fails closed
Assessment metadata, scope, and limitations ### Metadata - Target repository: `github/gh-aw-firewall` - Analyzed commit: `360f0f904b1824dbffa1288d8dee58db94e903ab` - Target snapshot source: local `target/` checkout plus bounded GitHub metadata reads - Source verification date: `2026-10-13` - Final SSDF baseline used: `NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 (final, February 2022)` - Official URLs: - `https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/ssdf` - `https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final` - `https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218` - Machine-readable marker: - `` ### Scope and assumptions - Repository-observable review only: committed files in `target/` and bounded accessible GitHub metadata. - Assessed against the current final SSDF baseline above. The NIST SSDF project page also references `SP 800-218A` as a final SSDF community profile for generative AI and dual-use foundation models, but it augments `SP 800-218` and was **not** treated as a replacement baseline for this repository review. - Findings are risk-based and scoped to evidence visible in this repository snapshot; absence of repository evidence is **not** proof that an organizational control does not exist. ### Inaccessible or non-repository evidence - Branch protection / rulesets details were not readable with the available credential (`gh api repos/github/gh-aw-firewall/branches/main/protection` returned `403 Resource not accessible by personal access token`). - GitHub security feature state, private security alerts, secret-scanning alerts, advisories, internal training records, personnel/process evidence, and private incident-response artifacts were not assessed. - Workflow files provide evidence of intended controls, but this run did not establish historical execution success for every workflow.
PO / PS / PW / RV practice-to-evidence matrix ### Practice matrix | Practice / task focus | Status | Repository-observable evidence | Evidence limits / assumptions | Concrete improvement and risk reduced | |---|---|---|---|---| | `PO.1.1`-`PO.1.3` — define and communicate software-development security requirements | `PARTIAL` | `docs/security.md` defines disclosure expectations; `docs/awf-config-spec.md`, `docs/network-isolation-design.md`, and `docs/image-verification.md` document security-relevant product and release requirements; `README.md` surfaces supported security behaviors. | No visible organization-wide policy register, annual review record, or third-party acquisition/security-contract evidence. | Consolidate repository-scoped secure-release requirements for CLI and container artifacts in one maintained policy/doc so release obligations do not drift. Reduces missed integrity requirements. | | `PO.2.1`-`PO.2.3` — roles, responsibilities, training, leadership commitment | `HUMAN_REVIEW_REQUIRED` | `.github/CODEOWNERS` assigns a maintainer; `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/security.md` define contributor/security reporting paths. | Training, management commitment, and role review cadence are not repository-observable. | Maintain explicit code ownership and review paths; confirm separately whether secure-development roles and training are formalized. Reduces reliance on implicit ownership. | | `PO.3.1`-`PO.3.3` — supporting toolchains and artifacts | `OBSERVED` | `.github/workflows/codeql.yml`, `dependency-audit.yml`, `supply-chain-scan.yml`, `test-coverage.yml`, and `release.yml` codify automated checks; actions are commit-pinned; release artifacts include `checksums.txt`, `containers.txt`, and schemas. | Runtime hardening and monitoring of hosted CI infrastructure itself are not directly visible. | Preserve pinned-action and artifact-producing workflows; add equivalent provenance coverage for CLI assets. Reduces toolchain tampering blind spots. | | `PO.4.1`-`PO.4.2` — criteria for security checks and protected evidence | `PARTIAL` | High/critical dependency findings fail in `.github/workflows/dependency-audit.yml`; PR-built container CVEs fail in `supply-chain-scan.yml`; coverage regressions fail in `test-coverage.yml`; CodeQL runs on push/PR/schedule. | Criteria exist across workflows, but I did not find one central repo doc that ties gates, exceptions, and approval criteria together. | Keep machine-enforced thresholds close to the workflows and document exceptions centrally when they are allowed. Reduces inconsistent triage. | | `PO.5.1`-`PO.5.2` — secure development environments and hardened endpoints | `PARTIAL` | `docs/network-isolation-design.md`, `docs/security.md`, and product docs describe isolated execution, deny-by-default egress, and credential isolation patterns; several workflows use `persist-credentials: false` and least-privilege `permissions`. | Developer endpoint hardening, MFA, runner segmentation, and operational monitoring evidence are mostly outside the repository. | Continue isolating credentials and minimizing runner permissions; verify separately that endpoint and runner hardening matches the documented model. Reduces environment compromise exposure. | | `PS.1.1` — protect code and configuration from unauthorized access/tampering | `PARTIAL` | `.github/CODEOWNERS` exists; workflow actions are SHA-pinned; repository uses GitHub workflow files and code review paths typical for controlled changes. | Repository ACLs, branch protection, and mandatory review enforcement could not be confirmed with the available credential. | Verify rulesets/branch protection separately and keep CODEOWNERS current. Reduces unreviewed change risk. | | `PS.2.1` — provide a mechanism to verify software release integrity | `GAP_FOUND` | `docs/image-verification.md` documents cosign verification for container images. `install.sh` and release docs validate CLI assets with `checksums.txt`, and `.github/workflows/release.yml` generates that checksum file, but I did not find repo-observable signatures or provenance verification for `awf-*` binaries or `awf.tgz`. | There could be external verification material not visible here, but none was referenced in repository docs, workflows, or installer paths reviewed. | Publish and validate signed or attested verification material for CLI release assets. Reduces risk that a tampered binary and matching checksum on the same release channel evade detection. | | `PS.3.1`-`PS.3.2` — archive releases and maintain/share provenance | `PARTIAL` | `.github/workflows/release.yml` publishes binaries, tarballs, schemas, `checksums.txt`, and `containers.txt`; container images are signed and SBOM-attested; some enclave/cloud-hypervisor artifacts include provenance files. | Equivalent provenance/signature coverage for all CLI assets was not found. Long-term archive controls beyond GitHub Releases are not visible. | Extend provenance/signature publication from selected artifacts to the CLI release set. Reduces incomplete release-forensics coverage. | | `PW.1.1`-`PW.1.3` — design to meet security requirements and mitigate risks | `OBSERVED` | `docs/network-isolation-design.md`, `docs/security.md`, `docs/authentication-architecture.md`, `docs/sandbox-design.md`, and `docs/enclaves-architecture.md` capture security architecture and threat-model reasoning. | This does not prove that every change receives formal threat modeling. | Preserve design docs and keep threat-model updates coupled to security-relevant changes. Reduces design drift. | | `PW.2.1` — independent review of design against security requirements/risk | `PARTIAL` | `.github/CODEOWNERS` supports review; `.github/workflows/security-review.md` exists as a dedicated threat-model/security review workflow; release/process docs contain review-oriented checks. | Could not confirm mandatory execution or independence for every design-affecting change. | Define when security design review is required and link resulting artifacts to changes. Reduces missed design regressions. | | `PW.4.1` / `PW.4.2` / `PW.4.4` — acquire, maintain, and verify reused software/components | `OBSERVED` | `.github/dependabot.yml` updates npm, Docker, and GitHub Actions dependencies; `dependency-audit.yml` and `supply-chain-scan.yml` verify dependency risk; `package-lock.json` and `docs-site/package-lock.json` lock dependencies. | Supplier assurance outside what is codified in repo tooling is not visible. | Keep automated update + audit loops in place and include new ecosystems as they are added. Reduces stale dependency exposure. | | `PW.5.1` — secure coding practices | `OBSERVED` | `package.json` includes `eslint-plugin-security`; source contains dedicated lint/test rules (for example `eslint-rules/no-unsafe-execa.js`); `codeql.yml` enables `security-extended,security-and-quality`. | Secure-coding training and review quality are not directly observable. | Preserve secure-coding automation and add targeted rules when new risk classes emerge. Reduces recurring implementation flaws. | | `PW.6.1`-`PW.6.2` — hardened compilation/interpreter/build configuration | `OBSERVED` | `release.yml` pins actions, signs container images with cosign, generates SBOMs, disables cache for security-critical agent image builds, and runs seccomp verification checks for agent images. | Build-host hardening and provenance for all non-container binaries were not fully visible. | Extend hardened-build outputs with CLI-asset provenance/signatures. Reduces build artifact substitution risk. | | `PW.7.1`-`PW.7.2` — review/analyze human-readable code | `PARTIAL` | `codeql.yml`, ESLint security rules, `.github/CODEOWNERS`, and numerous tests provide automated/static review layers. | Mandatory human review enforcement could not be confirmed via rulesets/branch protection. | Keep static analysis current and validate human-review enforcement separately. Reduces code-level vulnerability escape. | | `PW.8.1`-`PW.8.2` — test executable code and record findings | `OBSERVED` | `test-coverage.yml`, `build-test.md`, smoke/test workflows, integration/unit tests in `package.json`, and security-focused scan workflows show extensive executable and workflow-level testing. | I did not inspect historical issue-tracking linkage for every discovered failure. | Preserve fail-closed security tests and keep coverage focused on security-critical paths. Reduces regression risk. | | `PW.9.1`-`PW.9.2` — secure settings by default | `OBSERVED` | `README.md` and design docs describe deny-by-default egress and credential-isolation defaults; product docs consistently position isolation and allowlisting as baseline behaviors. | Runtime deployment choices in consuming environments can still weaken defaults; that is outside repository-only proof. | Continue documenting safe defaults and test them in CI smoke flows. Reduces insecure deployment-by-default risk. | | `RV.1.1`-`RV.1.3` — identify and confirm vulnerabilities continuously | `OBSERVED` | `docs/security.md` defines disclosure intake; `codeql.yml`, `dependency-audit.yml`, and `supply-chain-scan.yml` run on push/PR/schedule; Dependabot is enabled. | Private bug bounty, advisories, and security alert triage data were not accessible. | Keep scheduled detection and disclosure intake active; ensure alert owners are explicit outside the repo snapshot. Reduces time-to-detection. | | `RV.2.1`-`RV.2.2` — assess, prioritize, and remediate vulnerabilities | `PARTIAL` | Failing workflows on high/critical findings and coverage regressions show repository-level prioritization logic; release docs and issue references in design notes show remediation work is tracked in source history. | SLA, prioritization rubric, and exception governance are not repository-observable. | Document remediation ownership and exception handling where repository contributors can see it. Reduces inconsistent response. | | `RV.3.1`-`RV.3.4` — root-cause analysis and SDLC improvement | `PARTIAL` | `.github/workflows/shared/self-hosted-failure-modes.md` records root causes, fixes, and validation guidance for recurring security/operational defects; tests and docs accompany many mitigations. | Could not confirm the same discipline for every security vulnerability class. | Continue codifying root causes and regression tests for security-relevant incidents. source_text:
Show HN: Koody for Business – AI bookkeeping for people who aren't accountants
Hi HN, I'm Hallie, founder of Koody. Today, I'm launching Koody for Business: AI-powered accounting, bookkeeping, and tax prep software for sole proprietors and small businesses. For years, I used accounting software for my business. I went into it to create invoices, categorize and reconcile transactions, and work with my accountant to prepare our books. I often dreaded having to do it. There were so many transactions to get through in a handful of different currencies, and I found the whole process draining. The software I used (and refuse to name) worked really well. It was capable accounting software, and I'm not trying to suggest otherwise. But for me, accounting had become a bit like going to the dentist. You know it's necessary and useful, but that doesn't stop you from feeling anxious about it or wishing you didn't have to go. What makes this personal is that I've always been good at accounting. Throughout secondary school, I was the best student in every financial accounting class. I was also the class prefect, so I would regularly collect everyone's homework and take it to the staff room for submission. My accounting teacher used to ask me to put mine on top because she used it as a marking guide. I then went on to study finance in undergrad and eventually earned an MBA. So accounting isn't an unfamiliar subject to me, yet dealing with my own books made me extremely sad and anxious. I'm building Koody for Business because I want business owners to see accounting through my original lens: something simple and enjoyable that doesn't require a degree to understand. Koody automatically categorizes business income and expenses and uses those transactions to produce cash flow insights, profit and loss reports, and records for Schedule C and tax prep. There are two workspaces: personal and business. The business workspace lets you manage your business finances separately from your personal finances, even when you use the same bank account for both, as many sole proprietors do. You can keep each transaction in the appropriate workspace, so personal spending stays out of your business reports. You can use Koody just for your business, just for your personal finances, or for both. Give Koody for Business a try at koody.com/business. I'd love to hear what you think.

TradeLink SEO automation — living project status, decisions and blockers
# Living project checkpoint: TradeLink SEO automation

_Last status checkpoint: 2026-10-16, late evening (Claude session, production-readiness pass). This issue is the canonical **working status** for future assistant/Claude handoffs. It is not authorization to publish. The detailed checkpoint is in the latest comment below._

## Objective and permanent operating rules
- Build a **real research-driven SEO agent** for TradeLink (`usetradelink.com`), combining Google Search Console, Semrush, verified competitor research and authentic TradeLink product facts.
- Prioritize **qualified traffic, conversions and measurable results**, not page count, keyword stuffing or AI-detection evasion.
- When authorized, the agent researches, audits, drafts, tests, proposes and creates PRs automatically. **Every public website change requires a new, specific human approval** before publication.
- Keep `PUBLISHING_ENABLED=false` until every step before step 15 of [`docs/ops/activation-checklist.md`](https://github.com/ThomasPeakBot/usetradelink/blob/claude/festive-lamport-7ttt72-release-automation/docs/ops/activation-checklist.md) is done.
- Never expose secrets, spend more API units, merge, or deploy public website changes without explicit authorization. **Semrush: no further billable requests.** Every path is now fail-closed (see #19).

## Evidence and review
- [Full-repository audit, issue #10](https://github.com/ThomasPeakBot/usetradelink/issues/10)
- Test results come from Claude's local runs (Postgres 16) **and** GitHub Actions CI.
- The **real-deployment check** (`deploy-verify`) runs on GitHub's runners against the actual Cloudflare preview of each PR.
- Railway, Slack, Search Console and live Semrush are **not** verified: Claude's sandbox cannot reach them.

#8, #9, #11, #12, #13, #15, #16 and #17 are fully contained in #18/#19; `git merge-base --is-ancestor` was checked for every head. Do not merge them separately. Close them once #18 and #19 are merged.

## Activation status (full ordered list: `docs/ops/activation-checklist.md`)
- **NEEDS MY APPROVAL:**
  - Cloudflare build → `_site`
  - Merge #18, then #19
  - Proposals #20–#22
  - Arm publishing
  - Engine-opened PRs
  - Semrush budget
  - Claude drafting
  - Product-claim decisions
- **NEEDS CONFIGURATION:**
  - Import the `main` ruleset
  - Railway source branch `main` + Wait for CI + PR Environments off
  - Create `seo-engine` and `seo-dashboard`
  - Read-only DB role
- **BLOCKED (owner must confirm):**
  - Current Railway variables
  - Search Console service-account access
  - Slack PB Assist round trip

## Product-owner decisions needed
1. **NinjaTrader:** the homepage FAQ says it's supported; everything else says Tradovate only. Blocked in the facts registry.
2. **"Ten protection rules":** on the homepage, in `llms.txt` and in the TradeSyncer comparison. #20 removes it from the Tradovate guide. The quality gate now catches it in table cells too.
3. **Competitor claims:** re-verify the TradeSyncer trial and annual discount, and the Tradecopia trial, then cite each one inline. Campaign item 5.
4. **Tracking/consent:** unchanged; needs a separately scoped approval.

## Handoff convention
For **each substantive project update made with an assistant**, update the status in this issue:
- date
- factual code and deploy state
- linked PR, CI and evidence
- decisions and approvals
- unresolved blockers
- next action

When a prior status becomes outdated, update it rather than representing it as current. Never claim work was applied if it was only proposed, and do not assume future automatic updates from other sessions or tools.

[wildcard] Kill the human-written repro: a self-submitting soundness pipeline (grammar fuzz → accept-gate → emit → go build → shrink → auto-file)
### The idea, in a paragraph

Hybrid already owns every piece of a machine bug-hunter except the machine. A grammar-driven generator can synthesize well-formed `.hy` programs by the million; `hyb check` filters the ones it ACCEPTS; the emitter lowers them; `go build` is an independent oracle that requires zero trust in our own code; a delta-debugging shrinker reduces any accepted-but-unbuildable program to a minimal repro automatically. Chain those five stages and the Tier-0 BUILDABLE guarantee stops depending on humans noticing violations: every violation becomes a one-command, minimized, self-filed issue — the first night it runs, the pipeline does mechanically the work of every soundness report filed here so far. It doubles as a regression gate in CI (fuzz for N minutes per PR) and as the corpus's missing half — the corpus proves the checker is right where we looked; the fuzzer proves it is right where we didn't. Any second oracle (`go vet`, the ownership runtime's own assertions, a checker derived from GUARANTEES.md rows) turns the same shape into a differential soundness engine.

### Which assumption it breaks

Two sacred cows. (1) *"Reproduction is the only door to a payout"* — the door today is a human-written repro; this removes the human from the loop, so reproduction becomes the toolchain's own output, not a reporter's skill. (2) *"A green corpus is our evidence of soundness"* — a fixed corpus only samples the program space; a fuzzer searches it, so the evidence stops being "we checked these programs" and becomes "we continuously searched for counterexamples and found none (N programs, M CPU-hours, coverage X)". The BUILDABLE claim in GUARANTEES.md goes from asserted to falsified-or-surviving, in public, with a number attached.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Every issue in this tracker is a human finding a hole once, a fix closing it, and the next hole waiting for the next human. This changes what the project *is*: soundness stops being a property people verify occasionally and becomes a property the toolchain attacks continuously. It also inverts the trust debate the other wildcard families are having — capabilities (W-001–W-004), the untrusted emitter (#345), native-Go analysis (W-011–W-013) all argue about which component to trust; a pipeline checked against the real Go toolchain is the only argument that does not have to trust the checker, the emitter, or the alias graph *at the same time*. A normal feature bounty would reject it — no user-visible feature, pure tooling; this track exists exactly for that.

**Why now — receipts from this repo's own week.** Three distinct defect classes slipped past the standing evidence base — 191 unit tests, ~60 integration suites, a 1523/0 battery, a 109/109 differential corpus: (a) the sub-64 constant-conversion over-rejection pinned by `tests/const_conversion.rs::sub64_integer_overflow_folds_and_stays_accepted` — it broke while sitting in an open fix PR (#907); (b) pointer-parameter auto-addressing pinned by `tests/pointer_borrow_chains_issue_131.rs` — same story (#911); (c) the four range-bound bypass classes of #827. Each surfaced only because a human happened to write one more case — and two of them survived even the fix authors' own validation loops until a full-suite run forced them out. `check → emit → go build` finds every one of these classes mechanically, before a fix ships, on every commit. Meanwhile the tracker is absorbing waves of instant, unverified issues (dozens per afternoon): triage bandwidth, not report supply, is the bottleneck — and the pipeline's output is the opposite of that noise: every auto-filed report arrives already verified (accepted + unbuildable) and delta-minimized.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Preregistered spike, scoped to `spikes/<id>-self-submitting-pipeline/` (ID from triage):

1. **Build** (no checker/emitter changes): grammar+corpus-seeded generator, driver, delta-debug shrinker.
2. **Budget**: ≥3 nights × ~16 CPU-hours — order 10^4–10^5 fully-compiled programs (check → emit → `go build`) and ~10^6 checker-only programs per night.
3. **Negative control first**: seed the pipeline with the known pre-fix vectors (#827's six loops, the sub64 accept set) against the pre-fix commit — it must re-find them; without this, a silently broken oracle reads as saturation.
4. **SUCCESS** = ≥1 accepted-but-unbuildable minimal repro on current main — filed immediately as a first-reporter soundness issue (P0-class insights bypass the review calendar per MOONSHOT.md).
5. **SATURATION** = 0 findings after the full budget — the first *measured* bound on how saturated the checker is, something no fixed corpus can state. Either outcome publishes as the M2 learning; both are paid.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

No checker or emitter code changes — external tooling only (generator, driver, shrinker, ~1–2k lines) plus CI wiring. What breaks: CI minutes (tunable N per PR), triage load (needs a dedup label and a rate cap, e.g. ≤5 auto-filed issues/week), and Go becomes a CI dependency for the oracle (already pinned: go1.26.9). User-facing migration: none.

### Track terms

- [x] I understand no prototype is required and failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome
- [x] I understand all outcomes (including declines and failures) are published in MOONSHOT.md

source_text:
AI Agent: Anthropic thinking block is duplicated across parallel tool calls, Anthropic API rejects the next turn with 400 "Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block"
### Bug Description

When an Anthropic Chat Model with thinking enabled (explicitly, or by default on Claude Sonnet 5 / Opus 5.x, which think adaptively when no `thinking` field is sent) returns **one `thinking` block followed by two or more `tool_use` blocks in the same response**, the AI Agent node (Tools Agent V3) fails on the very next model call:

```
400 {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"messages.1.content.3: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block. The block is bound to a different conversation. Remove the block, or set `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior` to \"drop_block\". That setting requires the `thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01` value in the `anthropic-beta` header. This request has content before this block that was not present when it was created, first at `messages.1`."}}
```

Surfaced in n8n as `NodeOperationError: Bad request - please check your parameters` on the AI Agent node, thrown from `ToolsAgent/V3/helpers/executeBatch.ts`.

Turns with a single tool call work. The failure only happens when the model issues parallel tool calls, so it is intermittent and depends on the model's choice.

### Root cause (verified in source on master @ 40094e3, 2026-10-15; reproduced on 2.42.7)

The model returns a single assistant turn shaped like `[thinking, tool_use A, tool_use B]`. The thinking block carries a signature that Anthropic binds to that exact turn.

When the agent rebuilds the history after running the tools:

1. `createEngineRequests.ts` → `extractThinkingMetadata()` (line 43) copies the same `thinkingContent` / `thinkingSignature` into the metadata of **every** tool action of the batch. In the saved execution both actions carry an identical `metadata.anthropic.thinkingSignature`.
2. `buildSteps.ts` → `buildSteps()` (line 345) builds the steps. For Gemini it detects parallel calls sharing a thought signature and merges them into one assistant message via `buildSharedGeminiAIMessage()` (lines 288 and 389–412). There is no equivalent branch for Anthropic. Each Anthropic tool call goes through `buildIndividualAIMessage()` (line 236) → `buildAnthropicContentBlocks()` (line 93), which always returns `[thinkingBlock, toolUseBlock]` (line 126).

The history sent on the next call is therefore:

```
Human: ...
AI:   [thinking(sig S), tool_use A]
Tool: result A
AI:   [thinking(sig S), tool_use B]      <- same signature S, replayed under a different prefix
Tool: result B
```

Anthropic now validates that a signed thinking block is replayed under the prefix it was created with. The second copy is preceded by `tool_use A` and `result A`, which did not exist when the signature was minted, so the request is rejected. The comment above the Gemini branch in `buildSteps.ts` describes exactly this problem ("Splitting into separate model turns invalidates the signature"); the Anthropic path simply never got the same handling.

### Related

- #40360 (open) touches the same Anthropic replay path in `buildSteps.ts`.
- #38302 (merged) made empty-text thinking blocks survive the round-trip. This report is the next failure after that fix: the block survives, but it is duplicated.
- #37730 / #37954: explain why thinking is on by default for Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 when Thinking Mode is unset.

### To Reproduce

1. Workflow: Manual Trigger → **AI Agent** (Tools Agent, typeVersion 3.1).
2. Chat model: **Anthropic Chat Model** (typeVersion 1.6), model `claude-opus-5-5` (or `claude-sonnet-5`), **no Thinking Mode option set** (so the model thinks adaptively), or Thinking Mode: Adaptive.
3. Attach two independent tools, e.g. two HTTP Request Tool nodes, or one MCP Client Tool exposing several tools.
4. Prompt with something that invites two lookups at once, e.g. "Look up the user with email X AND search for similar tickets about Y, then summarise."
5. When the model answers with one thinking block and two `tool_use` blocks, both tools run, and the next Anthropic Chat Model call fails with the 400 above. Open the execution → Anthropic Chat Model → second run → input: the history shows `AI: [thinking][tool_use]` twice with the same signature.
6. Prompt it so that it only calls one tool per turn: works.
7. Set Thinking Mode: Disabled, or switch to the OpenAI Chat Model: works.

In my instance this hit 5 production runs in ~24 h on a support-ticket agent with an MCP Client Tool (`get-user` + `find-users`, `get-user` + `get-invoices`, `find-users` + `find-teams`, …). In every failing run, both actions in `subNodeExecutionData.actions[].action.metadata.anthropic` had the identical `thinkingSignature`.

### Expected behavior

Parallel Anthropic tool calls from a single thinking turn should be replayed as **one** assistant message `[thinking, tool_use A, tool_use B]` followed by the tool results, the same way `buildSharedGeminiAIMessage()` already does for Gemini thought signatures. Alternatively, the thinking block should be attached only to the first tool call of the batch and omitted on the others.

### Workarounds

- Set **Thinking Mode: Disabled** on the Anthropic Chat Model node (works since #37954; not possible on models that cannot disable thinking).
- Use a different chat model node.

BENCH-SPACE-004: quantify supplier concentration versus cislunar service resilience
## Research basis

The OECD's 2026 Space Economy at a Glance assesses a space economy whose access has broadened while launch activity, orbital infrastructure and supply chains remain concentrated. It reports that four providers accounted for more than four-fifths of orbital launches in 2025 in one commonly used metric and highlights single-country dependencies in crucial space-related inputs. See https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-space-economy-at-a-glance-2026_cbf9b240-en/full-report/managing-vulnerabilities-dependencies-and-sustainability-risks-of-the-space-economy_4d97ef6d.html

These real-world observations motivate this benchmark; the fixture values below are synthetic and must not be presented as the OECD's provider shares or as an actual procurement dataset.

## Paradigm shift

Treat supplier diversity as a measurable resilience attribute with an explicit cost—not as a slogan and not as a proxy for arbitrary failure probabilities. Compare the cost of a concentrated procurement portfolio with the additional cost of a portfolio that can still meet its service floor after any one supplier fails.

## Synthetic reference case

Required service demand: 70 normalized capacity units.

- Concentrated portfolio capacities: 50, 20, 15, 15 (total 100); listed lifecycle procurement cost: 100 synthetic cost units; portfolio HHI: 3,350 using the sum of squared percentage shares.
- Diversified portfolio capacities: 25, 25, 25, 25 (total 100); listed lifecycle procurement cost: 118 synthetic cost units; portfolio HHI: 2,500.
- Under concentrated sourcing, losing the 50-unit provider leaves 50, below the demand floor of 70 (shortfall 20). Losing any smaller provider leaves at least 80.
- Under diversified sourcing, losing any one 25-unit provider leaves 75, satisfying demand 70.

The 18% diversification premium is the explicit trade-off in the toy case, not a real cost estimate. Deterministic fault cases do not imply that outages are equally likely or independent.

## Required invariants

1. Compute HHI from the fixture's declared capacity shares; require shares to be non-negative and sum exactly to 100% (or use an explicitly documented normalized unit).
2. Run every single-supplier failure as a separate deterministic case; do not assign outage probabilities without evidence.
3. Calculate remaining capacity, unmet demand, lifecycle cost and the service-floor result for every case.
4. If N-1 supplier resilience is a hard requirement, mark the concentrated option infeasible before ranking price; select the cheapest feasible option only after gates.
5. Report cost, HHI, capacity and service separately—no composite score may hide a hard shortfall.
6. A higher HHI is not itself proof of market power or a causal failure probability; this is a procurement exposure metric over the specified candidate portfolio.
7. Reject a claimed robust portfolio if demand is raised above the remaining capacity after its weakest single-supplier failure.

## Acceptance targets

- 100% of named single-supplier fault cases have an independently recomputed remaining-capacity result.
- Zero infeasible options may win a hard N-1 gate on the basis of lower price.
- Exact HHI outputs match the analytical oracle (3,350 and 2,500 for the frozen fixture).
- Zero probabilistic-risk claim from deterministic fault coverage.
- Reports show diversification premium, capacity shortfall and HHI side-by-side.

## Composition

This is a new synthetic portfolio slice linked to the [Space Economy Reference Benchmark Suite PR #1736](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/pull/1736) and the [common-cause resilience work #1749](https://github.com/Luminous-Dynamics/symtropy/issues/1749). It should compose with Symtropy's deterministic market/logistics models and Mycelix provenance, with Symthaea comparing policies and Sol Atlas projecting supply and dependency context. It is not a second generic market engine.

source_text:
Show HN: Flopper is a hardware explorer for AI infrastructure and beyond
Hello! I built Flopper to make it easier to compare GPUs and understand the tradeoffs for workloads for AI and beyond. When researching GPUs from say Nvidia, AMD, and Huawei, I kept running into the same problem: specs were scattered across datasheets, and matching them to available configurations, vendors, and prices was cumbersome and a bit weird and frankly annoyingggg! AMD made me make an account :( So I started a place to bring that information together. Flopper lets you compare GPU specs, including TDP and compute throughput in terms of flops/tops, alongside estimates for AI workloads or other compute workloads (say, ~FP32 based) I recently added pricing data from dozens of providers to help track how prices change over time. Getting reliable quotes for systems like the NVL72 is still particularly difficult tbh, not sure how I can tell you how much that costs easily due to them being behind large procurement contracts and big multi-nationals. One thing that's become fairlyyyy clear is the interest in consumer cards and local LLMs. The bigger challenge is connecting advertised specs to real-world performance. In our testing so far, I’ve seen roughly 85% of advertised throughput, but that’s a ballpark observation for the workloads I’ve tested, not a general rule and so variable (power, cooling, workload etc). I'm considering a CLI that lets people run benchmarks and submit results, potentially using MLPerf as an automation? That way, we can all compare quoted performance with the workload, configuration etc. I'd love feedback: what information is missing, how can I improve it? And what would you need to see to trust a community-submitted benchmark? Corrections and additions also very welcome - some of the measurements are best efforts (and simple multiplications) but I hope it's of some use. Thanks for looking :)

**Release gate:** owner-validated sanitized ORIGINAL export (at least one for each distinct launch supplier ERP/file layout), verified price/discount meaning and brand policy, catalog sample, approved logo/packshot source rights. Synthetic fixtures never count as real export evidence; mark BLOCKED if absent, don't invent success. How Does the Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT NAND Flash Memory Work?
NAND flash memory is an essential technology in modern electronic systems, providing non-volatile data storage that retains information even when power is disconnected. It is widely used in embedded systems, automotive electronics, industrial equipment, and digital devices that require reliable memory solutions.
The Micron [MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT](https://globx.eu/products/micron/mt29f1g08abafah4-aatf) NAND Flash Memory is a 1Gb single-level cell (SLC) NAND flash memory device designed for applications that need dependable data storage and parallel memory access. With an 8-bit data bus, a 3.3V I/O interface, and an operating temperature range of -40°C to +105°C, it is suited to demanding embedded and automotive environments.
Understanding how this NAND flash memory works helps engineers select appropriate storage components for electronic system design, firmware storage, and industrial applications.

**What Is the Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT?**
The MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT is a non-volatile [NAND flash memory](https://doodleordie.com/profile/globxoffical) component manufactured by Micron Technology. It stores digital information in memory cells that retain their programmed state without continuous electrical power.
The device provides a 1-gigabit storage capacity, organized as 128M × 8 bits. Its parallel interface allows a compatible processor or memory controller to transfer data through an eight-bit bus.
Unlike volatile memory such as SRAM and DRAM, NAND flash memory preserves stored information when the system shuts down. This makes it useful for storing firmware, configuration data, and other information required when an electronic device starts operating.

**How Does NAND Flash Memory Work?**
NAND flash memory stores information by controlling the electrical charge within specialized semiconductor memory cells. These cells represent digital data through different electrical states.

The MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT uses single-level cell technology, meaning each memory cell stores one bit of information.
Its operation can be understood through three main processes.

1. Storing Data in Memory Cells
During programming, the memory device applies controlled electrical conditions to place charge into the storage structure of selected memory cells. The resulting electrical characteristics represent the programmed data.
In SLC NAND flash, each cell represents either a logical 0 or a logical 1. Because each cell stores one bit, SLC technology offers a straightforward storage arrangement compared with multi-level NAND technologies.
This design is useful in embedded applications where predictable memory behavior and endurance are important considerations.

2. Reading Stored Information
When a processor needs information, it sends the appropriate command and address to the NAND flash memory. The device accesses the selected location and determines the stored bit values by sensing the electrical characteristics of the memory cells.
The retrieved data is transferred through the eight-bit parallel interface.
A compatible controller or processor coordinates the read operation and uses the returned information for tasks such as loading firmware, accessing configuration settings, or retrieving stored program data.

3. Erasing and Reprogramming Data
NAND flash memory generally erases data in blocks rather than allowing arbitrary individual bytes to be overwritten directly.
When existing information must be replaced, the system typically erases the relevant block before programming new data into it. Pages are used for read and program operations, while blocks contain multiple pages.
The controller or firmware must manage these operations correctly, including handling bad blocks and monitoring data integrity where required.

**What Makes SLC NAND Flash Different?**
Single-level cell NAND flash stores one bit per memory cell. Other NAND technologies, including MLC, TLC, and QLC, store multiple bits per cell.
The main difference is how many electrical states each cell must distinguish.
SLC NAND uses two principal states, making the interpretation of stored data simpler than in technologies that use more states per cell. SLC memory is therefore often selected for applications that prioritize endurance, reliable operation, and consistent embedded storage behavior.
However, actual performance and endurance depend on the device specifications, operating conditions, and the system's memory management strategy.

**Applications of the Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT**
The combination of SLC NAND technology, parallel access, and an extended operating temperature range makes this memory component relevant to several types of electronic systems.

**Automotive Electronics**
Automotive electronic control units may need non-volatile storage for firmware, calibration information, and configuration data. A memory device rated for operation from -40°C to +105°C can be considered for suitable automotive designs, provided all electrical, qualification, and reliability requirements are satisfied.

**Industrial Embedded Systems**
Industrial controllers, monitoring equipment, and automation systems often need persistent storage for program code and system settings. NAND flash memory can provide this storage without requiring continuous power.

**Firmware and Boot Storage**
Embedded platforms can use NAND flash to store firmware images and other startup information. The processor or bootloader must support the memory interface and the device's command and timing requirements.

**Communication and Control Equipment**
Networking devices, industrial communication modules, and electronic control products may use parallel NAND memory for firmware and data storage. The suitability of this specific device depends on capacity requirements, controller compatibility, and the application's reliability targets.

**Advantages of the Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT**
Several characteristics make this component worth considering during embedded memory selection.

**Non-volatile storage**: Stored information remains available when the power supply is disconnected.
SLC memory architecture: One bit per cell provides a simpler storage scheme and is commonly associated with higher write endurance than higher-density multi-bit NAND technologies.

**Parallel data interface:** The eight-bit bus supports data transfer to compatible memory controllers and processors.
Extended temperature range: The specified -40°C to +105°C operating range supports designs exposed to a broad range of environmental temperatures.

**Compact package:** The 63-ball VFBGA package helps integrate memory into space-constrained electronic designs.
These benefits must be evaluated alongside the full datasheet, system architecture, and application-specific requirements.

**Design Considerations Before Using This NAND Flash Memory**
Selecting a [flash memory](https://support.cookiebot.com/hc/en-us?brand_id=360000562514) component involves more than checking capacity and voltage. Engineers should verify several technical factors before integrating the MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT into a design.

First, confirm that the processor or NAND controller supports the device's command set, addressing scheme, bus timing, and electrical interface.

Second, check whether error correction is required. NAND flash can develop bit errors, so the controller may need suitable error-correction code (ECC) capabilities. Do not assume that all error correction is handled internally; verify the exact device documentation.

Third, consider bad-block management, wear management, data retention, and power-loss behavior. These factors are particularly important in products that store firmware or frequently update persistent information.

Finally, confirm the package footprint, voltage limits, environmental requirements, and the exact ordering suffix. Components with similar part numbers may have different package, temperature, or electrical characteristics.

**Why Choose a Suitable NAND Flash Memory Supplier?**
Finding the correct memory component is an important part of reliable electronic product development. Engineers and procurement teams should evaluate manufacturer documentation, traceability, component condition, and availability before purchasing semiconductor memory.

For engineers researching embedded memory solutions,[ globX](https://globx.eu/) provides an online platform for exploring electronic components and sourcing requirements. Buyers can also visit the[ globX electronics blog](https://globx.eu/blog) for additional information about semiconductor devices, component specifications, and electronic sourcing topics.
Always verify the exact part number and its current datasheet before making a purchase or approving a component for production.

**Conclusion**
The Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT NAND flash memory provides 1Gb of non-volatile SLC storage through an eight-bit parallel interface. Its 3.3V I/O specification, compact VFBGA package, and extended operating temperature range make it relevant to compatible embedded, industrial, and automotive electronic designs.
Understanding NAND programming, reading, erasing, and memory-management requirements helps engineers determine whether this component meets their system's storage needs. For accurate implementation, always consult the manufacturer's datasheet and verify interface compatibility, error-correction requirements, and operating conditions.
Explore electronic components and sourcing information at[ globX](https://globx.eu/) to support your next electronic design or procurement project.

**Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)**
1. What is the Micron MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT?
It is a 1Gb SLC NAND flash memory device with an eight-bit parallel data interface, designed for non-volatile storage in compatible electronic systems.
2. How much data can this NAND flash memory store?
Its nominal capacity is 1 gigabit, equivalent to approximately 128 megabytes of raw binary storage.
3. Does the MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT retain data without power?
Yes. NAND flash is non-volatile memory, so it retains stored information without continuous electrical power, subject to specified data-retention conditions.
4. What is SLC NAND flash memory?
SLC stands for single-level cell. It stores one bit per memory cell and is commonly used where endurance and dependable embedded storage are important.
5. What is the operating temperature range of this device?
The manufacturer's specifications list an operating temperature range of -40°C to +105°C.
6. What interface does this Micron memory use?
It uses a parallel NAND interface with an eight-bit data bus. The host processor or memory controller must be compatible with the device's electrical and timing requirements.
7. Can NAND flash memory be overwritten directly?
Typically, NAND flash must be erased in blocks before the affected storage can be reprogrammed. The host system must manage erase and program operations correctly.
8. Is the MT29F1G08ABAFAH4-AAT suitable for automotive electronics?
Its extended temperature range makes it a candidate for suitable automotive applications. Engineers should still confirm the exact ordering code, qualification requirements, and system-level compatibility before use.

source_text:
Show HN: Daisy – macOS software KVM with native trackpad gestures
I have three laptops on my desk most days.  Each laptop is used for different work, that I need to keep separate.  (Day job, advisory work, personal.)  When I went looking for a software KVM, the only free one that correctly handled trackpad gestures was Apple's Universal Control but that requires using the same iCloud account on each system, which is a non starter. I had planned to just contribute to something else but the best option I found was intended to be a universal software KVM and had already rejected OS specific features.  I get the thinking and don't begrudge the devs at all but I needed something that supports my workflow.  Thus, Daisy (as in "daisy chain"). Daisy is a FOSS software KVM for macOS that doesn't need an iCloud account and handles gestures the way I want it to.  You arrange the displays to match your physical desk, move the pointer across an edge, and control follows it to the next machine. Nothing leaves the local network (unless you want auto-updates) and there's encryption all the way around anyway. It turns out that getting the trackpad working is somewhat non trivial. macOS doesn't expose Spaces and Mission Control swipes through the public gesture events. They arrive as private DockControl events, which meant figuring out how to capture the gesture phases, progress, and velocity, transport them, and replay them on another Mac. There's a fair amount of undocumented macOS behavior involved, and I've documented what I figured out in the repo. Beyond gestures, the key things I wanted: - Capable of handling a large chain (8), with a layout tool that that makes it easy to arranges systems the way they exist on my desk
- Copy/paste across machines for images, files, and folders
- No accounts or other external dependencies
- Keeping displays active across the whole chain when you're doing work, without violating the intent behind screen locking
- No single machine acting as the control system that all peers must negotiate with for trust (the machine you're typing on is always the control system) It's not quite 1.0. Occasionally the layout UI loses track of a peer even though the connection is fine, input can sometimes get jerky, and I still need to beat on file transfers more. I use it daily, though, and it's reached the point where I find it genuinely useful. It currently requires Apple silicon and macOS 26 or later. I've tested on 26 and 27. Code, downloads, and the technical documentation are here:
 https://github.com/misfitdev/daisy  I'd be particularly interested in hearing from anyone who's fought with macOS input events or tried to solve the same problem. And if you give Daisy a shot, I'd like to know what breaks. I'm also really happy about the security design and I'd love for people to poke holes in it. :)

WPF XPS synthetic hyperlinks exposed through UI Automation can bypass restrictive navigation checks and reach attacker-controlled content, enabling remote code execution after user interaction.

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/471
